MACHINE LEARNING FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES · LECTURE 09 / 12

Dimensionality Reduction: PCA, SVD, t-SNE & UMAP

How do we understand data with hundreds of features when we can only visualize two or three dimensions?

In Lecture 8, we explored unsupervised learning. K-Means grouped observations around centroids, DBSCAN discovered dense regions, and Gaussian Mixture Models represented overlapping clusters probabilistically.

But all our examples used just two features.

Now imagine clustering 10,000 research papers, each represented by a 768-dimensional sentence embedding.

We can't visualize 768 dimensions. Worse, some dimensions might contain redundant information, irrelevant variation, or noise.

What if we could compress the data into fewer dimensions while retaining its most useful structure?

That's the motivation for dimensionality reduction.

Today, we'll connect five ideas: PCA, eigenvectors and SVD, explained variance, nonlinear visualization with t-SNE and UMAP, and anomaly detection.

1. Why reduce dimensions in the first place?

Imagine describing a person using three measurements:

  • Height in centimeters

  • Height in inches

  • Weight in kilograms

Do we really have three independent pieces of information?

No. Height in centimeters and height in inches describe exactly the same underlying quantity.

One dimension is redundant.

A similar problem occurs in real datasets.

For instance, suppose our features include house size, number of rooms, and total floor area. These may be strongly correlated.

Dimensionality reduction attempts to create a smaller representation that preserves useful information from the original features.

768D

Original embedding

2D

Visualization

A reduction to two dimensions is useful for plotting, but it generally loses some information.

Dimensionality reduction can help with visualization, compression, denoising, faster downstream learning, and mitigating problems caused by high-dimensional distances.

But there's an essential distinction:

Reducing dimensions does not always preserve the information needed for your actual task.

A direction containing little overall variation might still be extremely important for predicting a rare class. We'll return to that caveat.

2. PCA: Find the most informative viewing angle

Let's begin with Principal Component Analysis (PCA), one of the most important classical dimensionality-reduction techniques.

Imagine a collection of two-dimensional points that forms an elongated cloud.

We want to replace each point's two coordinates with just one number.

Which direction should we project the points onto?

Here's the intuition:

Choose the direction along which the observations vary the most.

Why?

If we project the cloud along its longest direction, its observations remain relatively spread out and distinguishable.

If we project it from the wrong angle, many different points collapse to similar positions.

Interactive: Discover the first principal component

The blue points represent observations with two correlated features.

Rotate the green line. Every point is projected onto it, shown by the green markers. The dashed connectors show how far the original observations are from their projections.

Your objective: Find the angle that preserves the greatest amount of variance.

What should you notice?

When the line aligns with the cloud's longest direction, we retain almost all its variation.

When the line becomes perpendicular to that direction, much of the variation collapses.

PCA automatically finds the best direction without us manually rotating anything.

That direction is called the first principal component (PC1).

The second principal component (PC2) is perpendicular to the first and captures the greatest remaining variance.

The third does the same after the first two, and so on.

3. PCA, eigenvectors, and eigenvalues — without the heavy mathematics

These terms sound intimidating, but their roles in PCA are simple.

Eigenvectors — The directions

They tell PCA which directions correspond to the principal axes of the data's covariance structure.

Eigenvalues — How much variance

Each principal eigenvector has an eigenvalue telling us the amount of variance along that direction.

Here's a small example.

Suppose PCA finds these component variances:

Component

Eigenvalue

Explained variance

PC1

7

70%

PC2

2

20%

PC3

1

10%

Total variance = 10.

Keeping PC1 alone preserves 70%.

Keeping PC1 and PC2 preserves 90%.

So we can reduce a three-dimensional dataset to two dimensions while retaining 90% of its overall variance.

The essential terminology

  • Principal components: New axes, ordered by variance captured.

  • Explained variance ratio: Proportion of total variance captured by each axis.

  • Cumulative explained variance: Total proportion captured by the first K axes.

  • Component scores: The new coordinates of observations after projection.

In compact notation, PCA projects a centered observation onto its chosen axes:

z=Vk⊤(x−μ)\boxed{z=V_k^\top(x-\mu)}

You don't need to derive it. It just means: subtract the dataset mean, then express the observation using the K retained directions.

One subtle point: Variance isn't necessarily usefulness

PCA is unsupervised. It doesn't know your labels or what you're trying to predict.

A feature direction with low variance might still separate an important rare class.

So keeping 95% of the variance does not guarantee keeping 95% of the information relevant for classification.

That distinction matters when using PCA before supervised learning.

4. SVD: The mathematics powering PCA

You might have seen Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in linear algebra or deep learning.

Its connection to PCA is especially useful.

SVD breaks a matrix into three parts:

Xc=UΣV⊤\boxed{X_c=U\Sigma V^\top}

where XcX_c is our centered data matrix.

For PCA, think of the decomposition like this:

Part

Intuition

V⊤V^\top

Directions of the principal components

Σ\Sigma

Strength of the variation along those directions

UU

How observations contribute to those directions

The singular values in Σ\Sigma are closely related to the covariance eigenvalues: squaring a singular value and dividing by n−1n-1 gives the corresponding variance.

Why should you care?

Because SVD is a practical way to compute PCA without explicitly forming and diagonalizing the covariance matrix.

It's also useful in matrix compression, low-rank approximation, and latent semantic analysis.

SVD is a general matrix factorization; PCA is a particular dimensionality-reduction procedure that can use it.

For example, if a matrix of 1,000 document vectors has shape:

X:(1000,768)X:(1000,768)

we might retain the first 50 principal components:

Z:(1000,50)Z:(1000,50)

Each document is now represented by 50 numbers rather than 768.

The price is information loss, but if the discarded directions primarily contain redundancy or noise, the compressed representation may still be useful.

For sparse TF-IDF document matrices, TruncatedSVD is often preferable because it can operate without the centering performed by ordinary PCA.

5. The limitation of PCA: What if the data is curved?

PCA is a linear dimensionality-reduction method.

It finds straight axes.

But suppose data lies along a curved surface, like a rolled-up sheet of paper.

The data might have three coordinates, even though its underlying structure is essentially two-dimensional.

Curved manifold

The structure bends through the original space.

Unfolded representation

A nonlinear representation can preserve local relationships.
Conceptual illustration of manifold learning, not an exact embedding produced by an algorithm.

A linear projection can flatten different parts of a curved structure onto each other.

So what if, instead of preserving maximum variance along straight axes, we tried to preserve which observations are neighbors?

That leads to t-SNE and UMAP.

6. t-SNE: Keep similar observations together

t-Distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding (t-SNE) is especially popular for visualizing high-dimensional data in two dimensions.

Its guiding intuition:

If two observations are similar in the original high-dimensional space, try to place them near each other in the visualization.

It constructs similarities between observations in the original space and looks for a low-dimensional layout with corresponding local similarities.

Unlike PCA, it isn't restricted to a linear projection.

Imagine visualizing sentence embeddings

Suppose we have 1,000 embeddings of scientific abstracts.

Some discuss:

  • Argument mining

  • Machine translation

  • Information retrieval

A t-SNE visualization might reveal regions where similar abstracts appear near one another.

But there's a crucial warning.

t-SNE is primarily a visualization tool, not proof that distinct real-world clusters exist.

A plot with five visible islands does not necessarily mean the dataset contains five objectively meaningful categories.

t-SNE can exaggerate apparent separation, and distances between different islands are often not reliable measures of original-space similarity.

The main hyperparameter: Perplexity

Perplexity roughly controls the neighborhood scale that t-SNE uses when comparing observations.

Lower perplexity

Higher perplexity

Emphasizes more local relationships

Uses a broader neighborhood scale

Can reveal fine-grained groupings

Can emphasize broader patterns

May become sensitive to small fluctuations

May smooth over local detail

There's no universally optimal value. We should compare visualizations across reasonable settings and random seeds.

Also, standard scikit-learn TSNE provides fit_transform, but not a general transform method for projecting new observations onto an existing map.

7. UMAP: Another way to preserve neighborhood structure

Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is another nonlinear dimensionality-reduction technique.

Conceptually, it tries to preserve relationships between nearby observations by constructing a neighborhood graph in the original space and finding a low-dimensional representation that reflects those relationships.

It can be used for visualization and, with appropriate validation, as a learned transformation for downstream tasks.

Two settings are particularly important.

n_neighbors — How local should the representation be?

A smaller value emphasizes fine local structure.

A larger value considers broader neighborhoods and may better reflect some global structure.

min_dist — How tightly can points pack together?

A smaller value allows compact, tightly packed groups in the visualization.

A larger value encourages observations to spread out more.

Smaller min_dist

Tighter visual groups

Larger min_dist

More spread-out groups
Conceptual illustration of how packing can change; not the output of a particular UMAP fit.

UMAP can often be efficient and offers a way to transform new observations using a fitted reducer.

However, just like t-SNE, its two-dimensional visualization can distort original distances and apparent cluster sizes.

Changing n_neighbors, min_dist, the distance metric, or the random seed can alter the plot significantly.

PCA vs. t-SNE vs. UMAP

PCA

t-SNE

UMAP

Main idea

Preserve maximum variance along linear axes

Preserve local similarities

Preserve neighborhood structure

Linear?

Yes

No

No

Good for

Compression, preprocessing, visualization

Exploratory visualization

Visualization, nonlinear embeddings

New observations

Straightforward transform

Not with standard sklearn TSNE

Supported by fitted UMAP models

Interpretability

Components are linear combinations of features

Plot axes aren't directly interpretable

Plot axes aren't directly interpretable

Main caveat

Can discard low-variance predictive information

Visual islands can mislead

Visual distances and clusters can mislead

An important practical rule:

Use PCA when you want a simple, reproducible compression method. Consider t-SNE or UMAP when you want to explore nonlinear structure visually.

Neither t-SNE nor UMAP is automatically a better replacement for PCA in a predictive pipeline.

8. Let's compare all three methods in Python

We'll use scikit-learn's handwritten digits dataset.

Each image is 8 × 8 pixels, so every digit is represented by 64 numerical features.

We'll compress those 64 dimensions and visualize what the algorithms discover.

Python

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE

# 1. Load handwritten digits: 64 pixel features
X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)

# Use a reproducible subset for quick visualization
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
idx = rng.choice(len(X), 600, replace=False)

X = X[idx]
y = y[idx]

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)

# 2. PCA: retain 95% of total variance
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95, svd_solver="full")
X_reduced = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)

print("Original dimensions:", X.shape[1])
print("Reduced dimensions:", X_reduced.shape[1])
print("Variance retained:",
      pca.explained_variance_ratio_.sum())

# 3. PCA visualization: 2 dimensions
pca_2d = PCA(n_components=2)
Z_pca = pca_2d.fit_transform(X_scaled)

# 4. t-SNE visualization
Z_tsne = TSNE(
    n_components=2,
    perplexity=30,
    init="pca",
    learning_rate="auto",
    random_state=42
).fit_transform(X_reduced)

# 5. UMAP visualization (optional dependency)
# Install first with: pip install umap-learn
views = {"PCA": Z_pca, "t-SNE": Z_tsne}

try:
    import umap

    Z_umap = umap.UMAP(
        n_components=2,
        n_neighbors=15,
        min_dist=0.1,
        random_state=42
    ).fit_transform(X_reduced)

    views["UMAP"] = Z_umap

except ImportError:
    print("Install umap-learn to include UMAP.")

# 6. Compare visualizations
fig, axes = plt.subplots(
    1, len(views), figsize=(5 * len(views), 4)
)

if len(views) == 1:
    axes = [axes]

for ax, (name, Z) in zip(axes, views.items()):
    ax.scatter(
        Z[:, 0], Z[:, 1],
        c=y, cmap="tab10", s=12
    )
    ax.set_title(name)
    ax.set_xticks([])
    ax.set_yticks([])

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

How should you interpret the plots?

With PCA, you may observe substantial overlap between digit classes. This is because two linear directions cannot necessarily capture everything distinguishing the digits.

With t-SNE or UMAP, different digits may form clearer visual groupings because the algorithms try to preserve nonlinear neighborhood relationships.

But remember: the labels are used only to color the plot, not to fit the dimensionality-reduction models.

And clearer-looking clusters don't automatically mean that an embedding contains more useful information for a classifier.

Practical PCA tip: How many dimensions should we retain?

Instead of always choosing two components, we can choose a variance-retention target.

For example:

Python
pca = PCA(n_components=0.95, svd_solver="full")

This tells PCA to keep enough components to explain at least 95% of the observed total variance.

It's a useful heuristic, not a universal optimum. If PCA is part of a supervised model, the number of components should ideally be selected using validation performance.

Also, fit PCA and preprocessing on training data only when using them in a predictive pipeline, to prevent leakage. For pure exploratory visualization of a dataset, fitting on the displayed observations is normal.

Part III — Anomaly Detection

9. Can dimensionality reduction help us detect unusual observations?

We've discussed compressing data and visualizing its structure.

But consider another possibility.

Suppose our observations normally follow a strong relationship:

y≈0.7xy\approx0.7x

Most observations lie close to that line.

Now we encounter a new observation far from it.

Could its distance from the learned pattern indicate an anomaly?

Yes. This is one application of PCA reconstruction error.

How does PCA reconstruction work?

Recall that PCA projects an observation onto a lower-dimensional representation.

We can also approximately transform that compressed representation back into the original feature space.

If we retained only one principal component, the reconstruction lies on the learned one-dimensional line.

The difference between the original observation and its reconstruction is called reconstruction error.

What did we learn?

An observation that fits the learned low-dimensional relationship reconstructs relatively well.

An observation far away from that relationship has a large reconstruction error.

For PCA-based anomaly detection, the basic workflow is:

Learn PCA from representative normal data

↓

Compress and reconstruct new observations

↓

Measure reconstruction errors

↓

Flag unusually large errors

A simple Python version:

Python

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Normal observations approximately follow y = 0.7x
x = rng.uniform(-3, 3, 300)
X_normal = np.column_stack([
    x,
    0.7*x + rng.normal(0, 0.2, len(x))
])

# Learn the main direction from normal data
pca = PCA(n_components=1)
pca.fit(X_normal)

def reconstruction_error(X):
    compressed = pca.transform(X)
    reconstructed = pca.inverse_transform(compressed)
    return np.mean((X - reconstructed)**2, axis=1)

# Illustrative threshold from training errors
train_errors = reconstruction_error(X_normal)
threshold = np.quantile(train_errors, 0.99)

new_points = np.array([
    [1.5, 1.0],   # Near the normal pattern
    [1.5, -2.5]   # Far from the normal pattern
])

for point, error in zip(
    new_points, reconstruction_error(new_points)
):
    print(
        point,
        "Error:", round(error, 3),
        "Flagged:", error > threshold
    )

The threshold here is just a teaching example based on the upper 1% of training errors. In a real application, we'd validate thresholds using suitable held-out data and consider the cost of false alarms.

Is PCA the best anomaly detector?

Not always.

PCA reconstruction error is useful when normal observations follow an approximately low-dimensional linear structure.

But an anomaly can sometimes lie along the principal direction, far outside the usual range, while still reconstructing very well.

So PCA reconstruction error may miss some unusual observations.

Other popular methods include:

Method

Main intuition

Isolation Forest

Anomalies tend to be isolated using fewer random splits

Local Outlier Factor (LOF)

Compare a point's local density with that of its neighbors

One-Class SVM

Learn a boundary surrounding typical observations

PCA reconstruction error

Flag observations that don't fit a learned linear subspace

Autoencoder reconstruction error

Use a learned nonlinear representation to identify poorly reconstructed observations

The correct method depends on what makes an observation abnormal in the application.

10. Which dimensionality-reduction method should you use?

Your goal

Good starting choice

Compress 100 numerical features into fewer dimensions

PCA

Compress sparse TF-IDF document vectors

TruncatedSVD

Visualize high-dimensional embeddings

PCA, then potentially t-SNE or UMAP

Explore nonlinear neighborhood relationships

t-SNE or UMAP

Find a reusable nonlinear embedding for new data

UMAP, with proper validation

Detect points that violate an approximately linear pattern

PCA reconstruction error

Detect isolated anomalies in general tabular data

Isolation Forest as a baseline

A final practical detail: feature scaling matters enormously.

PCA is sensitive to numerical scale because it maximizes variance. If one feature is measured in thousands and another is measured between zero and one, the larger-scale feature may dominate.

Standardization is often useful, though not automatically appropriate for every dataset or embedding type.

11. Understanding check

Q1. Why does PCA choose directions with the greatest variance?

Q2. If two principal components explain 92% of total variance, does that guarantee retaining 92% of the information needed for classification?

Q3. What is the relationship between PCA and SVD?

Q4. A t-SNE plot shows five clearly separated islands. Does that prove the data contains five true clusters?

Q5. Why might PCA reconstruction error fail to detect an observation extremely far along a principal direction?

Reveal answers

Answer key

1. To preserve as much of the data's total variation as possible when projecting it into fewer dimensions.

2. No. The discarded 8% of variance could contain highly predictive class information.

3. SVD is a matrix factorization used to compute PCA's principal directions and component strengths.

4. No. t-SNE's visual separation can be influenced by neighborhood settings, initialization, and distortions introduced by the projection.

5. Because the observation may still lie on the learned subspace and therefore reconstruct accurately, despite being unusual in its location along that subspace.

12. The bigger picture

High-dimensional observations

Many features, redundancy, possible noise

↓

PCA / SVD

Linear compression through dominant variance directions

t-SNE / UMAP

Nonlinear embeddings emphasizing neighborhood relationships

↓

Use the representation

Visualization · Compression · Clustering · Anomaly Detection

The four insights to remember:

1. PCA finds directions that preserve the most variance. Eigenvectors describe these directions, eigenvalues their strengths, and SVD provides a way to compute them.

2. t-SNE and UMAP focus on neighborhood relationships. They're valuable for exploring high-dimensional data, but their plots can distort distances and apparent clusters.

3. Dimensionality reduction and clustering are different tasks. One constructs a smaller representation; the other assigns groups. They can be used together, but shouldn't be confused.

4. Low-dimensional structure can support anomaly detection. Observations that don't fit learned patterns may be unusual, but the definition of an anomaly depends on the problem.

MACHINE LEARNING FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES · LECTURE 10 / 12

Practical ML Engineering

From messy, real-world data to reliable machine learning systems.

In our first nine lectures, we explored most of the foundational classical ML algorithms:

  • Supervised learning: Linear Regression, Logistic Regression, kNN, SVMs, Decision Trees, Random Forests, and Gradient Boosting.

  • Unsupervised learning: K-Means, DBSCAN, hierarchical clustering, Gaussian Mixture Models, and dimensionality reduction.

But our examples had one unrealistic advantage: the data was already clean.

In a real ML project, you might receive a customer dataset containing missing ages, inconsistent currencies, categorical values, duplicate users, highly imbalanced labels, and features that wouldn't be available when making a prediction.

You could have the world's best algorithm and still build a terrible model.

The central lesson today: the data pipeline and evaluation design are often just as important as the algorithm itself.

We'll build one complete example throughout this lecture: predicting whether a customer will leave a subscription service (customer churn).

1. The real-world problem: Raw data isn't ready for ML

Imagine receiving this dataset:

Customer churn dataset

Raw data

Age

Monthly €

Contract

Churn

24

29

Monthly

Yes

35

59

Annual

?

79

Monthly

Yes

42

?

Annual

No

29

49

Monthly

No

Illustrative observations. The question marks represent missing values.

Before we can train a model, several questions arise.

What should we do about missing values? How can a model understand "Monthly" and "Annual"? Should age and monthly charges be measured on comparable scales? What if only 10% of customers actually leave?

And most importantly: How do we make sure our preprocessing doesn't accidentally reveal information from the test set?

Let's tackle these issues in the order we'd encounter them in a real project.

2. Missing values: What should we do when information is absent?

Suppose 8% of our customers have no recorded age.

A machine learning model often cannot directly use these missing values.

We have several options.

Approach

Intuition

When useful

Drop rows

Remove observations with missing information

Few missing entries, dropping them won't introduce serious bias

Mean imputation

Replace missing values with the average

Numerical features without strong outliers

Median imputation

Replace with the middle observed value

Numerical features with skew or outliers

Most-frequent imputation

Use the most common category

Categorical features

Missingness indicator

Add a feature recording whether the value was missing

Missingness itself may carry useful information

Example: Why median can beat mean

Suppose the observed customer ages are:

[22, 24, 25, 27, 82][22,\ 24,\ 25,\ 27,\ 82]

The mean is 36, while the median is 25.

If one customer is missing their age, imputing 36 may be less representative of this particular group than imputing 25.

This doesn't mean median is always best. It means the treatment should reflect the distribution and task.

An important subtlety: Why is the value missing?

Missing values don't always occur randomly.

For example, suppose high-income customers are less likely to disclose their income. The missingness itself might be predictive.

Or perhaps a laboratory test is only ordered for patients with particular symptoms.

Blindly filling missing values can erase meaningful signals.

Practical default: For a simple numerical tabular baseline, try median imputation. For categories, try most-frequent imputation or an explicit "Missing" category, and investigate whether missingness indicators help.

We don't need to spend hours on imputation theory to understand the key principle: missingness is part of the data-generating process, not merely an inconvenience.

3. Categorical encoding: How does the model understand words?

Our dataset has a feature called Contract.

Possible values:

  • Monthly

  • Annual

  • Two-year

A numerical model cannot simply interpret these strings as meaningful quantities.

We need to encode them.

The problem with arbitrary numbers

We might try:

Contract

Encoded

Monthly

0

Annual

1

Two-year

2

But this introduces a numerical ordering and distance that may not make sense for a nominal category.

For example, Logistic Regression would treat this as one numerical feature, even though the categories aren't naturally separated by equal distances.

One-hot encoding

A common alternative is to create one binary column for each category.

One categorical column becomes three binary columns

Contract

Monthly

Annual

Two-year

Monthly

1

0

0

Annual

0

1

0

Two-year

0

0

1

Now the model can learn a separate effect for each category.

Other encoding strategies

Encoding

Intuition

Useful for

One-hot

Separate binary feature per category

Low/moderate-cardinality nominal features

Ordinal

Preserve a meaningful order

Education level, customer tiers

Frequency

Encode how frequently a category appears

High-cardinality categories

Target encoding

Use a smoothed label-based statistic per category

High-cardinality features, with careful leakage control

Native categorical handling

Let a compatible algorithm process categories

CatBoost, supported LightGBM/XGBoost configurations

The biggest warning is target encoding leakage.

If you encode a category using its average target calculated from all observations, you can accidentally reveal label information to the model.

Target encoding must be carefully fitted within the training process, typically with cross-fitting or suitable out-of-fold procedures.

For our churn example, we'll use the simpler and safer starting point: one-hot encoding.

4. Feature scaling: Does the algorithm care about units?

Consider two features:

Feature

Example range

Age

18–80

Annual income

€15,000–€150,000

Suppose we're using kNN, which classifies based on distance.

A difference of €20,000 in income could overwhelm a difference of 20 years in age, simply because of the numerical units.

This is why feature scaling matters.

The most common approach is standardization:

z=x−μσ\boxed{z=\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}}

It subtracts the feature's mean and divides by its standard deviation.

Which algorithms care about scaling?

Algorithm

Scaling usually needed?

Why?

Logistic / Linear Regression

Often beneficial, especially with regularization

Coefficient penalties and optimization

kNN

Yes

Distance calculations

SVM

Usually yes

Distances, margins, kernel behavior

K-Means / PCA

Usually important

Distances and variance

Decision Trees

Usually no

Threshold-based splitting

Random Forests

Usually no

Tree-based splits

Gradient-boosted trees

Usually no

Tree-based splits

Scaling doesn't automatically improve every algorithm.

For a tree, splitting on income < 40000 is equivalent in principle to splitting on the corresponding standardized threshold.

For kNN, scaling can completely change which observations count as neighbors.

The rule that prevents leakage

We calculate the scaler's mean and standard deviation using training data only.

Then we apply those same values to validation, test, and future observations.

Why?

Because a test set is supposed to represent unseen information.

Using it to calculate preprocessing statistics means our training procedure has already been influenced by evaluation data.

Let's make that visible.

5. Interactive: How preprocessing causes data leakage

Suppose our training set contains four monthly spending values:

[10, 12, 14, 16][10,\ 12,\ 14,\ 16]

Their mean is 13.

Now imagine the validation set contains one customer who spends 100.

If we calculate the mean using all five observations, we get 30.4.

That validation example has changed a statistic used by our model's training pipeline—even though it was supposed to be unseen.

The principle is simple:

Anything that learns information from the dataset must be fitted on the appropriate training partition, not on the held-out data.

That includes imputers, scalers, PCA, learned categorical encodings, feature selection and the prediction model itself.

6. Feature engineering: Creating better information

Now our data is clean and numerical.

But what if the available features aren't very informative on their own?

This brings us to feature engineering.

Feature engineering means creating or transforming inputs so that a model can learn useful relationships more easily.

Imagine we're predicting churn.

Raw data includes total_spending and tenure_months.

We might create:

Average monthly spending=Total spendingTenure months\text{Average monthly spending} = \frac{\text{Total spending}}{\text{Tenure months}}

Or perhaps:

Support ticket rate=Support ticketsTenure months\text{Support ticket rate} = \frac{\text{Support tickets}}{\text{Tenure months}}

These derived features may be more meaningful than the raw numbers individually.

Three common types of feature engineering

Ratios and interactions

Examples: debt-to-income ratio, price per square meter, or support tickets per month.

Time-based features

Examples: days since last purchase, average transactions over the past 30 days, or seasonality.

Representation transformations

Examples: log-transforming skewed amounts, polynomial features, TF-IDF, or embeddings.

The goal isn't to create hundreds of features. It's to create features that capture useful signals.

And every feature must be available at the moment the prediction is made.

For example, if we're predicting churn on November 1, we cannot use a customer's total purchases during November 1–30. That would be future-information leakage.

Feature engineering vs. feature selection

These sound similar, but they solve different problems.

Feature engineering creates or transforms information.

Feature selection chooses which available features to retain.

Feature selection method

Intuition

Filter methods

Rank features using statistics such as mutual information

Wrapper methods

Test subsets based on actual model performance

Embedded methods

Let the algorithm perform selection, e.g. Lasso

Permutation importance

Measure performance deterioration when a feature is shuffled

One warning: correlated features can make feature importance and selection unstable. And supervised feature selection must happen inside the training folds during cross-validation.

For tabular ML, I'd usually start with sensible domain features and a strong baseline rather than performing complicated feature selection immediately.

7. Class imbalance: When positive examples are rare

Let's say only 10% of customers churn.

If we predict "will not churn" for everyone, we get 90% accuracy while identifying zero departing customers.

We already saw this problem in Lecture 4.

Now let's look at the engineering solutions.

Strategy

What it does

Tradeoff

Class weighting

Gives minority-class mistakes more influence during training

Can increase false positives

Oversampling

Repeats or generates minority-class examples

Risk of overfitting or synthetic-data artifacts

Undersampling

Removes some majority-class examples

Discards potentially useful data

Threshold tuning

Changes the decision rule without retraining

Trades precision against recall

Suitable metrics

Evaluates what matters for the minority class

Requires matching metrics to real costs

Should we always balance the dataset?

No.

For example, if fraud occurs in only 1% of real transactions, artificially changing the training class balance can affect the model's raw probability estimates.

Class weighting can help classification decisions, but doesn't guarantee better calibrated probabilities.

Also, never blindly balance the test set. It should reflect the distribution relevant to deployment or to the evaluation question.

A useful starting approach: Try ordinary training first, compare class-weighted training, inspect precision/recall and PR-AUC, and tune the decision threshold on validation data.

Any resampling procedure must occur inside the training folds, not before the train/test split.

8. The complete leakage-safe workflow

Now let's assemble these ideas into a proper training pipeline.

Raw dataset

Audit features, missingness, duplicates and target definition

↓

Split: Train / Validation / Test

Before fitting preprocessing

↓

Numerical features

Impute missing values

↓

Scale if necessary

Categorical features

Impute missing categories

↓

One-hot encode

↓

Fit model and compare hyperparameters

Use training data and cross-validation where appropriate

↓

Select threshold and model

Using validation evidence and real-world objectives

↓

Final test evaluation

Untouched until model and decisions are finalized

Why pipelines are important

Doing all this manually in notebooks is error-prone.

One forgotten scaling operation or an imputer accidentally fitted on validation data can invalidate the evaluation.

Scikit-learn provides two especially useful tools:

ColumnTransformer applies different preprocessing operations to different columns.

Pipeline connects those transformations to the estimator, making it possible to fit and evaluate the whole workflow consistently. It also helps prevent leakage during cross-validation.

Let's use them in a real example.

9. Hands-on: Build a complete customer churn pipeline

Let's combine everything in one runnable experiment.

We'll create a realistic-looking synthetic customer dataset with numerical and categorical features, missing values, and an imbalanced churn target.

Then we'll train two Logistic Regression models—one with ordinary training and one with class weighting—and select a model and decision threshold using validation data.

Python

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler, OneHotEncoder
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import (
    accuracy_score, precision_score, recall_score,
    f1_score, average_precision_score, confusion_matrix
)

# 1. Generate synthetic customer data
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n = 2000

tenure = rng.integers(1, 73, n)
monthly = np.clip(rng.normal(65, 20, n), 15, 150)
tickets = rng.poisson(1.5, n)
age = rng.integers(18, 75, n).astype(float)

contract = rng.choice(
    ["Monthly", "Annual", "Two-year"],
    n, p=[0.5, 0.35, 0.15]
)
region = rng.choice(["North", "South", "East"], n)

# Generate the hidden churn probabilities
logit = (
    -2.7
    + 0.025 * (monthly - 65)
    + 0.35 * tickets
    - 0.025 * tenure
    + 0.9 * (contract == "Monthly")
    + 0.2 * (region == "South")
)

prob = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))
y = rng.binomial(1, prob)

X = pd.DataFrame({
    "age": age,
    "tenure_months": tenure,
    "monthly_charge": monthly,
    "support_tickets": tickets,
    "contract": contract,
    "region": region
})

# 2. Add a simple engineered feature
X["tickets_per_year"] = (
    12 * X["support_tickets"]
    / X["tenure_months"].clip(lower=3)
)

# 3. Introduce realistic missing values
X.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.08, "age"] = np.nan
X.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.06, "monthly_charge"] = np.nan
X.loc[rng.random(n) < 0.05, "region"] = np.nan

print("Churn rate:", round(y.mean(), 3))
print("Missing values:")
print(X.isna().sum())

# 4. Train / validation / test: 60% / 20% / 20%
X_dev, X_test, y_dev, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.20,
    stratify=y, random_state=42
)

X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_dev, y_dev, test_size=0.25,
    stratify=y_dev, random_state=42
)

numeric = [
    "age", "tenure_months", "monthly_charge",
    "support_tickets", "tickets_per_year"
]
categorical = ["contract", "region"]

# 5. Build fresh preprocessing for each model
def build_model(balanced=False):
    num_pipe = make_pipeline(
        SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True),
        StandardScaler()
    )

    cat_pipe = make_pipeline(
        SimpleImputer(strategy="most_frequent"),
        OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore")
    )

    preprocessing = ColumnTransformer([
        ("numeric", num_pipe, numeric),
        ("categorical", cat_pipe, categorical)
    ])

    return make_pipeline(
        preprocessing,
        LogisticRegression(
            max_iter=1000,
            class_weight="balanced" if balanced else None
        )
    )

# 6. Compare models and select thresholds on validation
candidates = {}

for name, balanced in [
    ("Standard", False),
    ("Class-weighted", True)
]:
    model = build_model(balanced)
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)

    val_probs = model.predict_proba(X_val)[:, 1]

    thresholds = np.arange(0.10, 0.91, 0.05)
    best_t = max(
        thresholds,
        key=lambda t: f1_score(
            y_val, val_probs >= t, zero_division=0
        )
    )

    val_f1 = f1_score(y_val, val_probs >= best_t)

    candidates[name] = (val_f1, model, best_t)
    print(name, "Validation F1:", round(val_f1, 3),
          "Threshold:", round(best_t, 2))

# 7. Select the winner without examining test results
winner = max(candidates, key=lambda name: candidates[name][0])
_, final_model, final_threshold = candidates[winner]

# 8. Final evaluation on untouched test data
test_probs = final_model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
test_pred = (test_probs >= final_threshold).astype(int)

print("\nSelected model:", winner)
print("Majority baseline accuracy:", round(1 - y_test.mean(), 3))
print("Test accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))
print("Test precision:", round(precision_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))
print("Test recall:", round(recall_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))
print("Test F1:", round(f1_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))
print("Test average precision:",
      round(average_precision_score(y_test, test_probs), 3))
print("Confusion matrix:")
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, test_pred))

This is runnable demonstration code, not a claimed execution. The data is synthetic, not actual customer records.

What's important about this code?

Not the exact scores. It's the design.

SimpleImputer learns missing-value replacements from the training set. OneHotEncoder learns categories and safely handles previously unseen categories. StandardScaler learns the appropriate training statistics.

class_weight="balanced" changes class contributions to the Logistic Regression training objective in inverse proportion to their observed frequencies.

All these transformations are fitted inside the pipeline. Validation and test data receive the already learned transformations without refitting them.

Our model is also evaluated against a majority-class accuracy baseline, so a high accuracy score alone doesn't fool us.

What happens when we deploy it?

We can use the fitted pipeline on a new customer:

Python

new_customer = pd.DataFrame([{
    "age": np.nan,
    "tenure_months": 8,
    "monthly_charge": 85,
    "support_tickets": 4,
    "tickets_per_year": 6.0,
    "contract": "Monthly",
    "region": "South"
}])

p_churn = final_model.predict_proba(new_customer)[0, 1]
decision = p_churn >= final_threshold

print("Estimated churn probability:", round(p_churn, 3))
print("Flag for retention outreach:", bool(decision))

The best part: we don't manually impute, scale or one-hot encode this new customer.

The pipeline performs the transformations in exactly the way learned from training.

That consistency is one of the most valuable reasons to use pipelines.

10. Splitting strategies: Random isn't always correct

Our code used random stratified splits, which are appropriate for many independent, exchangeable observations.

But imagine the data contains customer activity over several months.

If we're trying to predict future churn, a random split might mix observations from the future into training.

Or suppose we have five records from the same customer. Putting some into training and others into test can make evaluation unrealistically easy if our deployment goal is predicting for previously unseen customers.

Situation

Better splitting strategy

Independent classification records

Stratified random split

Multiple observations per customer

Group-based split

Predicting future behavior

Chronological split

Multiple hospitals, companies or datasets

Grouped or source-held-out evaluation

Generalization to a new domain

Explicit out-of-domain test set

The split should simulate the actual prediction conditions we care about.

This is a much deeper principle than simply remembering 80/20 or 70/15/15.

In particular, when evaluating cross-dataset generalization, random row splits may give misleadingly optimistic results because the training and test observations still share the same dataset-specific patterns.

11. Reproducibility: Could someone repeat your experiment?

We've used random_state=42 throughout our code.

That's a good start—but reproducibility goes beyond setting a seed.

A reliable ML experiment should preserve:

Reproducibility checklist

0 / 7

Dataset version and target definitionExact train / validation / test splitsFeature engineering and preprocessing choicesModel hyperparameters and random seedsPython and library versionsEvaluation metrics and decision thresholdsFinal model and experiment results

One especially useful habit is to record not only the best result but also the experimental choices that produced it.

For more complex experiments, saving metrics and configurations across multiple random seeds lets us examine whether an apparent improvement is stable or just due to random variation.

And a practical distinction worth remembering: reproducibility does not guarantee correctness. A model can reproducibly exploit leaked features or a flawed evaluation protocol.

12. The six common ML engineering mistakes

Mistake

Why it's dangerous

Scaling or imputing before splitting

Leaks evaluation information

Randomly splitting time-dependent data

May train on future information

Ignoring the majority-class baseline

Can make an ineffective classifier look impressive

Oversampling before cross-validation

Can leak duplicated or synthetic observations between folds

Selecting features on the entire labeled dataset

Gives feature selection access to held-out targets

Repeatedly tuning on the test set

Turns the test set into another validation set

Most of these errors can be avoided with carefully designed splits, pipelines, and evaluation procedures.

13. Understanding check

Q1. Why should we fit StandardScaler on training data only?

Q2. You're building a model with kNN and Random Forests. Which generally needs feature scaling more?

Q3. You're predicting customer churn using customer records from January through December. Your system will predict churn in January of the next year. Why might random splitting be misleading?

Q4. Does balancing the training data guarantee better probabilities or better F1?

Q5. What's the difference between feature engineering and feature selection?

Reveal answers

Answer key

1. Because using validation/test statistics to preprocess training observations leaks information and can bias evaluation.

2. kNN. Its predictions depend on distances; ordinary Random Forests generally don't depend strongly on feature units.

3. Random splitting can allow future behavior or temporal patterns to influence training, while deployment requires predicting later periods from earlier information.

4. No. Weighting or resampling changes the learning process and can improve minority recall, but may hurt precision or calibration.

5. Feature engineering creates or transforms predictive inputs. Feature selection decides which existing or engineered features to retain.

14. The bigger picture

Raw, imperfect data

↓

Prepare features

Imputation · Encoding · Scaling · Feature engineering

Protect evaluation

Correct splits · No leakage · Cross-validation

↓

Train and validate

Baseline · Algorithm · Hyperparameters · Threshold

↓

Evaluate, reproduce, deploy

Independent test performance and consistent processing

Four ideas to remember from today's lecture:

1. Data preparation is part of the model. Imputation, encoding, scaling, and feature transformations directly affect the predictions.

2. Feature engineering often matters more than trying increasingly complicated algorithms. Useful information has to be represented in a learnable form.

3. Evaluation design must match deployment. Chronology, grouping, class imbalance, and leakage can matter more than an extra percentage point of accuracy.

4. Pipelines make ML workflows safer and more reproducible. They connect preprocessing and modeling into one consistent process.

What if the customers change their behavior? What if our model is confident but wrong? What if the relationship between features and targets changes between datasets?

MACHINE LEARNING FROM FIRST PRINCIPLES · LECTURE 11 / 12

Reliability, Interpretability & Generalization

How do we know whether a model is trustworthy—and whether it will still work when the world changes?

In Lecture 10, we built a complete customer-churn prediction pipeline. We handled missing values, encoded categories, prevented data leakage, and evaluated our classifier on held-out data.

Suppose it achieves excellent test performance.

Are we finished?

Not quite.

Imagine deploying the model to thousands of customers. Immediately, several new questions appear:

  • Why is the model predicting that a customer will leave?

  • When it predicts 80% churn probability, can we trust that number?

  • What happens if customer behavior changes next month?

  • How do we know when the model needs attention or retraining?

These are the questions behind reliable machine learning.

Today's conceptual journey:

Interpretability

What is the model using, and why?

Uncertainty

How much should we trust its predictions?

Generalization

What happens on different data?

Monitoring

How do we detect problems after deployment?

Part I — Understanding What the Model Learned

1. Feature importance: Which inputs influence our predictions?

Remember our churn model. Its features included:

  • Customer tenure

  • Monthly subscription cost

  • Number of support tickets

  • Contract type

  • Region

Suppose it predicts that a customer is likely to churn.

We might want to know which of those features mattered most.

This introduces feature importance.

But there are two different questions we could ask.

Global explanation: Which features does the model generally rely on across many customers?

Local explanation: Which features contributed to the prediction for this particular customer?

Global

Contract

Tenure

Support tickets

Region

Local

Customer #1042

Monthly contract

Pushes prediction up

Long tenure

Pushes prediction down

Illustrative importance and contribution values, not measurements from our Lecture 10 model.

A global explanation gives an overview of model behavior.

A local explanation helps investigate an individual prediction.

Both are useful, but neither automatically tells us what causes churn.

For example, a model might rely heavily on region because region is correlated with something else. That doesn't mean changing a customer's region would change their behavior.

Predictive importance is not the same as causal importance.

2. Permutation Importance: What happens if we scramble a feature?

This method has a particularly intuitive interpretation.

Imagine we have a trained churn classifier with validation F1 = 0.80.

Now randomly shuffle the contract column, breaking the relationship between each customer and their actual contract.

Then evaluate the model again.

Suppose F1 drops to 0.58.

That suggests the model relied substantially on information in the contract feature.

Repeat for other features:

Feature shuffled

Illustrative F1 after shuffling

F1 decrease

None

0.80

—

Contract

0.58

0.22

Tenure

0.66

0.14

Support tickets

0.71

0.09

Region

0.79

0.01

This is Permutation Feature Importance.

The intuition:

Importance=Original score−Shuffled score\boxed{\text{Importance}=\text{Original score}-\text{Shuffled score}}

A larger performance drop indicates that disrupting that feature hurts the fitted model more, under the chosen evaluation setup. This works with models ranging from Logistic Regression to Random Forests and boosting.

But there's a catch: Correlated features

Suppose we have both monthly_spending and annual_spending.

They contain nearly the same information.

If we shuffle one, the model may still recover that information from the other. As a result, both can appear individually unimportant.

Permutation importance measures reliance on a particular feature given the other available features, not the feature's inherent usefulness.

When to use it: Start with permutation importance on held-out data when you want a relatively model-independent way to investigate global feature reliance.

3. SHAP: Why did this individual prediction happen?

Now let's go deeper.

Our model predicts that customer #1042 has a 55% probability of churn.

Instead of asking which features matter globally, we ask:

How did this customer's feature values move the model away from its baseline prediction?

That's the intuition behind SHAP — SHapley Additive exPlanations.

SHAP assigns contributions to input features relative to a reference or background prediction, using ideas from cooperative game theory.

Let's use a simple hypothetical example.

Suppose the model's baseline output is a logit of −1.2.

SHAP-style explanation for one customer

Baseline logit

-1.2

Monthly contract

+0.9

Support tickets

+0.7

Long tenure

-0.3

Region

+0.1

Final model logit

0.2

Corresponding sigmoid probability

55.0%

Illustrative additive contributions on the log-odds scale. Real SHAP values depend on the model, background distribution, explainer, and chosen output scale.

The feature contributions explain how we move from the reference output to the prediction.

In this example, monthly contracts and support tickets push the logit upward, while long tenure pushes it downward.

A useful distinction:

Permutation importance

SHAP

Commonly used for global importance

Can explain individual predictions and summarize globally

Measures performance drop after shuffling

Attributes contributions relative to a reference

Depends on the evaluation dataset and metric

Depends on the background and feature-dependence assumptions

Doesn't explain one exact prediction directly

Designed to decompose individual outputs

What SHAP cannot tell you

SHAP does not automatically establish causal effects.

If a feature receives a high positive SHAP value, that doesn't mean changing the feature would produce the corresponding change in a customer's behavior.

SHAP explains a model's prediction, not necessarily the mechanism of the real world.

Also, when features are correlated, credit allocation can depend substantially on how the explanation handles feature dependence.

Practical takeaway: Use SHAP to inspect and debug model predictions, but be cautious about interpreting explanations as causal recommendations.

Part II — How Much Should We Trust Predictions?

4. Prediction confidence is not the same as correctness

Suppose our churn model produces these probabilities:

Customer

Predicted churn probability

A

51%

B

80%

C

99%

It's tempting to say the model is most certain about customer C.

But a model can be 99% confident and completely wrong.

There are two important reasons predictions can be uncertain.

Aleatoric uncertainty — Inherent randomness

Two customers with identical recorded features might make different decisions because of unobserved personal circumstances. More data cannot completely eliminate this uncertainty.

Epistemic uncertainty — Limited model knowledge

The model might be uncertain because it hasn't encountered enough similar examples. Additional representative data or better modeling could potentially reduce this uncertainty.

This distinction is particularly useful for out-of-distribution examples.

A classifier may output 99% for a customer with features unlike anything it saw during training. That high output does not guarantee low epistemic uncertainty.

Standard softmax or sigmoid scores alone don't reliably separate these kinds of uncertainty.

Techniques such as ensembles, Bayesian methods, and conformal prediction can help quantify different aspects of uncertainty, though each comes with assumptions.

5. Calibration: Does 80% really mean 80%?

We introduced calibration in Lecture 4. Now let's see why it matters after deployment.

Imagine selecting 100 customers to whom our model assigned around 80% churn probability.

If approximately 80 of them actually churn, the predictions are well calibrated for that group.

If only 45 churn, the model is overconfident.

If 95 churn, it is underconfident.

Interactive: Three models with different probability quality

How do we improve calibration?

Two common methods are:

  • Sigmoid calibration: Fit a relatively simple mapping from the model's outputs to probabilities.

  • Isotonic regression: Fit a more flexible monotonic mapping, usually requiring more calibration examples.

Scikit-learn provides CalibratedClassifierCV, which can learn calibration using cross-validation instead of improperly fitting the calibration mapping on the same predictions used to train the base classifier.

Calibration is particularly important when predictions feed into decisions involving expected costs, risk estimates, or resource allocation.

A model can have excellent ROC-AUC but poor calibration. One measures ranking; the other measures probability reliability.

Part III — Generalization Beyond the Original Dataset

6. Distribution shift: What if the world changes?

Up to now, we've usually assumed our training and test observations come from approximately the same underlying distribution.

This is often called the i.i.d. assumption: observations are independent and identically distributed.

But the real world rarely remains perfectly stationary.

Suppose our churn model was trained on customers from 2024.

By 2027, prices, competition, customer behavior, and contract patterns may have changed.

Or perhaps we apply the model in another country with a different customer population.

This is distribution shift.

Training customers vs. new customers

Training population

New population

Illustrative change in the distribution of one feature. Detecting a change does not automatically establish that prediction performance has declined.

The key insight is that good performance on one dataset doesn't guarantee good performance on another dataset.

Three important types of shift

Shift type

What changes?

Example

Covariate shift

Input distribution P(X)P(X)

Customers in a new market have different income distributions

Label shift

Class proportions P(Y)P(Y), under the label-shift assumption

Churn becomes more common overall

Concept drift

Relationship P(Y∣X)P(Y\mid X)

A contract type that previously predicted loyalty no longer does

The distinctions matter because they suggest different remedies. Technically, strict covariate shift assumes P(Y∣X)P(Y\mid X) stays fixed, while strict label shift assumes P(X∣Y)P(X\mid Y) stays fixed. In practice, several kinds of shift can occur simultaneously.

An interactive concept-drift experiment

Imagine a model trained to estimate churn based on a customer's number of support tickets.

Initially, more tickets are associated with greater churn risk.

Now imagine a new customer-support policy changes that relationship.

The trained model hasn't changed, but the world has.

Even if the model was perfectly calibrated during training, it may no longer be calibrated after the relationship changes.

And without receiving new outcome labels, we might not even realize it immediately.

In-distribution vs. out-of-distribution evaluation

In-distribution (ID) evaluation measures performance on examples from approximately the same data-generating setting as training.

Out-of-distribution (OOD) evaluation tests whether learned relationships transfer to changed settings.

For example, in NLP:

  • Train on news articles, test on different news articles → relatively in-domain.

  • Train on news articles, test on scientific abstracts → cross-domain.

  • Train using one set of annotation guidelines, test using another → possible guideline or label-definition shift.

These settings can expose shortcuts the model learned from its original dataset.

This connects directly to our earlier discussion of data leakage: a model may appear excellent because it exploits familiar patterns that do not transfer.

7. Robustness: What happens when inputs are imperfect?

Distribution shift concerns changes in data populations or relationships.

Robustness more broadly asks whether a model behaves appropriately under perturbations, corruptions, or other realistic variations.

Consider a text classifier:

The service was surprisingly good.

Now change the sentence slightly:

Honestly, the service was surprisingly good!

A robust sentiment classifier would generally maintain the same interpretation.

But consider:

The service was not surprisingly good.

Now the meaning may have changed. We should not expect the same prediction.

So robustness does not mean forcing every altered input to produce the same output.

It means preserving behavior when the task-relevant meaning remains unchanged, while responding appropriately when meaningful information changes.

Practical robustness tests

For tabular ML, we might test missing features, measurement noise, unusual numerical values, and data from different regions.

For NLP, we might test paraphrases, formatting changes, spelling errors, domain transfer, and annotation-guideline changes.

For image models, realistic lighting, camera, compression and viewpoint changes may matter.

A useful distinction:

Robustness tests ask whether the system behaves correctly under specified changes. OOD tests ask how well it generalizes to shifted data distributions. These overlap, but aren't identical.

Part IV — Monitoring Models After Deployment

8. Model monitoring: How do we know when something is wrong?

Imagine your churn model has been deployed for six months.

At first, it performs well.

Then customer behavior begins changing. Perhaps a competitor launches a new subscription service, or the company's pricing policy changes.

The model continues producing predictions, but they may be becoming less reliable.

We need to monitor the system.

What should we monitor?

A model monitoring dashboard

Input quality

Missing values, unseen categories, changed feature distributions

Predictions

Score distributions, predicted class rates, unusual output changes

Performance

Recall, precision, calibration and error rates when labels arrive

Operations

Latency, error rates, throughput and service health

A useful monitoring graph might look like this:

Illustrative weekly ROC-AUC after deployment

Illustrative monitoring values, not actual model measurements.

The performance decline deserves investigation, but we shouldn't immediately assume concept drift.

Maybe the labeling process changed. Perhaps the data pipeline broke. Or the evaluation population is now different.

A sensible monitoring response

Detect an unusual change

↓

Investigate data quality, population and model performance

↓

Compare with a recent labeled baseline

↓

Decide whether to fix data, recalibrate, retrain or roll back

An important operational reality: input drift can be monitored without labels, but actual predictive performance usually requires observed outcomes.

In churn prediction, we might need to wait weeks to know whether a customer actually left.

That's why both unlabeled data monitoring and delayed outcome evaluation matter.

9. A compact Python experiment: Interpretability and distribution shift

Let's combine the most important concepts in one runnable example.

We'll create a binary classification problem, train Logistic Regression, inspect permutation importance, test calibration, and compare performance under changed data distributions.

Python

import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.calibration import CalibratedClassifierCV
from sklearn.inspection import permutation_importance
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score, brier_score_loss

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

def sigmoid(z):
    return 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z))

# 1. Original data: two predictive numerical features
X = rng.normal(size=(2400, 2))
p = sigmoid(1.5*X[:, 0] - 0.9*X[:, 1])
y = rng.binomial(1, p)

X_dev, X_test, y_dev, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.2, stratify=y, random_state=42
)
X_train, X_val, y_train, y_val = train_test_split(
    X_dev, y_dev, test_size=0.25,
    stratify=y_dev, random_state=42
)

# 2. Train our classifier
def build_model():
    return make_pipeline(
        StandardScaler(),
        LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)
    )

model = build_model()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 3. Global interpretability on validation data
importance = permutation_importance(
    model, X_val, y_val,
    scoring="roc_auc", n_repeats=10,
    random_state=42
)

print("Permutation importance (ROC-AUC drop):")
for i, v in enumerate(importance.importances_mean):
    print(f"Feature {i+1}: {v:.3f}")

# 4. Calibrate using cross-validation on training data
calibrated = CalibratedClassifierCV(
    estimator=build_model(),
    method="sigmoid",
    cv=5
)
calibrated.fit(X_train, y_train)

# 5. Evaluate original test distribution
def evaluate(name, X, y):
    probs = model.predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
    print(
        name,
        "ROC-AUC:", round(roc_auc_score(y, probs), 3),
        "Brier:", round(brier_score_loss(y, probs), 3)
    )

evaluate("Original test", X_test, y_test)

# 6. Covariate shift: input population changes,
#    but the true conditional relationship stays fixed
X_shift = rng.normal(
    loc=[1.4, 0], scale=[1, 1], size=(800, 2)
)
p_shift = sigmoid(1.5*X_shift[:, 0] - 0.9*X_shift[:, 1])
y_shift = rng.binomial(1, p_shift)

evaluate("Covariate shift", X_shift, y_shift)

# 7. Concept change on that same new input population
p_changed = sigmoid(-0.8*X_shift[:, 0] - 0.9*X_shift[:, 1])
y_changed = rng.binomial(1, p_changed)

evaluate("Changed relationship", X_shift, y_changed)

# 8. Compare probability calibration on original test data
raw_probs = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
cal_probs = calibrated.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]

print("Raw Brier:", brier_score_loss(y_test, raw_probs))
print("Calibrated Brier:", brier_score_loss(y_test, cal_probs))

What should you look for?

First, inspect which features permutation importance identifies as influential.

Then compare the original and shifted populations. Changing the input distribution does not necessarily cause worse performance; much depends on how the model behaves in the new regions.

Finally, changing the underlying relationship creates a mismatch between what the model learned and what the new labels represent.

Calibration may or may not improve the Brier score on this particular dataset. It should be evaluated rather than assumed beneficial.

This experiment illustrates an essential principle:

A model's reliability depends not only on how well it was originally trained, but also on whether the conditions under which it learned remain relevant.

Part V — Four Other Important ML Paradigms

We've covered the major foundational algorithms, but there are several highly practical areas worth connecting to the bigger picture.

We won't turn each into a separate lecture here. Instead, let's understand what makes each problem distinctive.

10. Time-Series Forecasting: Predicting the future

Suppose we want to predict tomorrow's electricity consumption.

We still have a regression problem, but now the observations have a meaningful chronological order.

The past influences the future.

Common feature ideas include previous values (lags), rolling averages, seasonal patterns and calendar variables.

A simple autoregressive model might look like:

y^t+1=w1yt+w2yt−1+b\hat y_{t+1}=w_1y_t+w_2y_{t-1}+b

This is just a regression model that uses previous observations as features.

More specialized approaches include ARIMA, exponential smoothing, boosted trees with lag features, and neural forecasting models.

The critical difference is evaluation: we cannot casually shuffle observations and train on future information. We need chronological evaluation or walk-forward validation.

11. Learning to Rank: Ordering results rather than classifying them

Imagine a search engine receives the query:

Best noise-cancelling headphones

Its objective isn't necessarily to classify each document as relevant or irrelevant independently.

It needs to rank the most useful results near the top.

Learning-to-rank systems may learn from relevance judgments, clicks or other feedback.

Common approaches include:

Approach

Intuition

Pointwise

Predict a relevance score for each result

Pairwise

Learn which of two results should rank higher

Listwise

Optimize the ordering of an entire result list

An important ranking metric is NDCG, which rewards placing highly relevant results near the top.

Other metrics include MRR, MAP, and Precision@K.

This connects naturally to Gradient Boosting: LightGBM and XGBoost support ranking objectives.

The key distinction is that ranking quality depends on the relative order of candidates for the same query, not merely their individual prediction errors.

12. Recommender Systems: Predicting preferences

Now imagine Netflix, Spotify, or an online shopping platform.

The system isn't simply predicting whether an item is positive or negative.

It's trying to discover which items a particular user is likely to enjoy.

Two foundational approaches:

Content-based filtering: Recommend items with attributes similar to those a user has liked.

Collaborative filtering: Use patterns of user–item interactions to discover shared preferences.

For example, if two users enjoy many of the same films, one user's favorites might be useful recommendations for the other.

More advanced systems use matrix factorization, learned embeddings, nearest-neighbor retrieval and neural ranking models.

One important practical complication is the feedback loop: users only interact with items the system chooses to show them. Observed clicks are therefore influenced by previous recommendations.

This creates exposure bias, making evaluation more complicated than ordinary supervised classification.

13. Online Learning: Updating as new data arrives

So far, our training workflow has looked like this:

Collect dataset → Train model → Deploy.

But what if data arrives continuously?

Online learning allows a model to update incrementally as new observations arrive.

For example, a spam filter might learn from newly labeled messages without retraining on its entire historical dataset every time.

Some scikit-learn estimators expose partial_fit() for incremental updates.

Online learning is useful for streaming data, changing patterns and systems where repeated full retraining is expensive.

But updating continuously introduces risks:

  • Learning from mislabeled or malicious examples.

  • Forgetting useful historical patterns.

  • Adaptation to temporary noise.

  • Evaluation leakage through poorly designed update sequences.

The important connection is that online learning addresses when and how the model updates, while the underlying model can still be linear, probabilistic, or another compatible algorithm.

14. Understanding check

Q1. A model assigns high importance to region. Does that prove region causally affects customer churn?

Q2. What is the difference between permutation importance and SHAP?

Q3. Your model has excellent ROC-AUC but consistently predicts 90% risk for events that occur only 60% of the time. What's wrong?

Q4. A model works well on English news but performs poorly on scientific abstracts. What general problem does this suggest?

Q5. You detect a major change in input feature distributions. Does that prove model accuracy has deteriorated?

Q6. Why is random train/test splitting often unsuitable for time-series forecasting?

Reveal answers

Answer key

1. No. The model may rely on region because of correlations or confounding. Predictive importance is not proof of causation.

2. Permutation importance measures performance degradation after shuffling a feature. SHAP attributes model-output contributions relative to a background reference.

3. Poor probability calibration, specifically overconfidence.

4. Domain or distribution shift, potentially exposing shortcomings in cross-domain generalization.

5. No. Input shift is a warning sign, but we need additional evidence—often new outcome labels—to establish a performance drop.

6. It can allow future observations to influence training, producing overly optimistic estimates of forecasting performance.

15. The bigger picture: From an accurate model to a reliable system

Train a model

Lessons 1–10: Algorithms, features, tuning and evaluation

↓

Understand

Feature importance · SHAP

Quantify reliability

Calibration · Uncertainty

Stress-test

OOD evaluation · Robustness

Monitor

Data drift · Performance · Operations

↓

Maintain a reliable ML system

Investigate changes, collect feedback, recalibrate or retrain when justified

The four ideas to remember from Lecture 11:

1. Interpretability is not causality. Feature importance and SHAP help explain what a model relies on, not necessarily why the real world behaves that way.

2. Confidence is not calibration. A high predicted probability isn't automatically trustworthy. We must evaluate whether probability estimates correspond to actual frequencies.

3. Generalization is a moving target. A model that performs well in one domain, population or time period may fail when conditions change.

4. Deployment is not the end of learning. Monitoring, feedback, stress testing and careful updates are part of building reliable ML systems.

Rather than introducing another collection of algorithms, we'll put everything together in a complete real-world problem.
